question: Russian has separate everyday words for light blue and dark blue. What did a 2007 test find this changes?
options: Russians tell some blues apart faster
answer: Russians tell some blues apart faster. Shown two shades on either side of their light-blue, dark-blue line, Russian speakers picked the matching shade slightly quicker; English speakers had no such edge. When a word task kept their language busy, the edge vanished. The words help sort colours, not see new ones.
move: Ask how big an effect is before believing how deep it goes.
ask: Which exciting claim have I repeated without asking how big the effect really was?
trap: They see shades others cannot, as if a word could create a colour.
reference: Winawer, Witthoft, Frank, Wu, Wade & Boroditsky, Russian blues reveal effects of language on color discrimination, PNAS 104(19), 2007
